items.message: The verb-parity test asserts each verb appears in GitLab and in the GitHub trampoline, but `in-lockstep gate` is only in the GitHub *implement* trampoline (`_SCAFFOLD_IMPLEMENT_TRAMPOLINE`), not in `_SCAFFOLD_TRAMPOLINE` (the review trampoline). The fallback to `_github_review_scaffold()` is the disjunction, so the assertion may pass even if `gate` is absent from `_SCAFFOLD_IMPLEMENT_TRAMPOLINE`, as long as `_SCAFFOLD_TRAMPOLINE` contains it — which is unlikely for the gate verb. The credential-split test asserts `'ANTHROPIC_IDENTITY_TOKEN' in work` by serialising the `work` job back to YAML and string-searching it. Because `id_tokens:` is a top-level key in the job dict (not in `script`), `yaml.safe_dump(parsed['work'])` will include it, so the assertion does exercise the right thing — but the comment says 'the work job has no way to reach a model' if it fails, when the actual mechanism being tested is the `id_tokens` key, not an environment variable or script line. The section-citation check searches `in-lockstep-design.md` for headings matching `^#+ (\d+(?:\.\d+)*) ` and compares against `§N.N` citations in gates.md. This will correctly catch the fixed pointer. No gap in the assertion itself — the test would fail if `§17.11` were not a real heading — but the test only checks citations that use the `§` prefix.
